drafts.title: The liquor cabinet is a furniture problem
drafts.educational_claim: A liquor cabinet is not a lifestyle accessory. It is a case that has to hold bottles, glass, and a person's habits without lying about water, weight, or light.

drafts.title: Three objects that keep getting one name
drafts.educational_claim: Cellarette, liquor cabinet, and built-in bar are three different assignments of movement, water, and the building. Using one word for all three is how rooms get the wrong object.

drafts.title: Who is talking, and what this shop will not invent
drafts.educational_claim: A custom furniture shop can teach bars as casework. It cannot narrate a plumbing license it does not hold or a celebrity cabinet that is not on the public record.

drafts.title: Wet, dry, cocktail, pantry — words that got stolen
drafts.educational_claim: Wet bar, dry bar, cocktail cabinet, and butler's pantry used to describe water, work, and a room. After lifestyle copy, they often describe a feeling.

drafts.title: Little cellars — the cellarette as a dining-room machine
drafts.educational_claim: A cellarette is a little cellar brought upstairs so bottles could live in the dining room, move to the table, and keep the evening from sending someone down the stairs.

drafts.title: Cisterns, coolers, and the metal that held the ice
drafts.educational_claim: Historic wine furniture is a wood case around a wet liner. The liner — lead, zinc, copper, sometimes marble — is the real climate. Lead is a museum fact, not a specification.

drafts.title: Adam's pedestals and the urn that was a bottle store
drafts.educational_claim: The 1760s dining-room set — side-table, pedestals, urns — hid bottle storage and plate-warming in architecture. The fitted sideboard was the smaller room's answer to that set.

drafts.title: Hepplewhite, Sheraton, and the cellaret sideboard
drafts.educational_claim: The 1788 Guide and Sheraton's Drawing-Book turned bottle storage into a drawn, repeatable sideboard interior — partitions, wells, plugs — that shops could build without inventing the form each time.

drafts.title: Why a wine box wanted to look like a tomb
drafts.educational_claim: Regency cellarettes often took the sarcophagus — a stone-coffin silhouette — because neoclassical taste dressed utility as antiquity. The grave look is style, not a secret meaning, and it still fights a dining-room chair.

drafts.title: Locks, decanters, and who kept the key
drafts.educational_claim: Historic drink furniture locked because wine was money and staffed houses leaked. A lock on a new cabinet is a household decision, not a speakeasy costume.

drafts.title: When the American dining room became a performance
drafts.educational_claim: Early-nineteenth-century American dining rooms grew as display rooms. The cellarette and sideboard are props in that performance, not extras.

drafts.title: Henry Sargent's Dinner Party — the cellarette in the picture
drafts.educational_claim: Sargent's 1821 Dinner Party at the MFA is primary evidence: a Boston dining room with the wine furniture at the table, working, not decorating.

drafts.title: New York, Boston, Charleston — regional cellarettes
drafts.educational_claim: American cellarettes shared a job and picked up regional shops, woods, and climates. A city name is not a personality. It is a workshop and a weather.

drafts.title: The sideboard as an American stage
drafts.educational_claim: The sideboard is the dining room's stage wall. In Federal and Empire America it held plate, linen, and a dock for the cellarette. A liquor cabinet that ignores the sideboard is ignoring the room's original bar.

drafts.title: Victorian carving and the bottle that hid underneath
drafts.educational_claim: Victorian sideboards kept the cellarette job and buried it under carving, plate, and mass. The bottles did not leave. They went downstairs in the piece.

drafts.title: The butler's pantry is a wet room, not a lifestyle
drafts.educational_claim: A historic butler's pantry is a service room between kitchen and dining — sink, china, glass, silver. The modern revival is often display. Keep the jobs from swapping clothes.

drafts.title: A lockable cabinet before anyone called it rebellious
drafts.educational_claim: Lockable drink furniture existed for a century as ordinary inventory control. Prohibition did not invent the lock. It changed what the lock was lying about.

drafts.title: Prohibition as a design brief
drafts.educational_claim: From January 17, 1920, to December 5, 1933, some households asked furniture to look ordinary. That is a brief. It is not a license to invent a nation of trick bookcases.

drafts.title: Bookcases, radios, and furniture that practiced looking innocent
drafts.educational_claim: Concealment furniture borrowed the silhouettes already in the parlor — bookcase, radio, sideboard — because innocence is a shape people already trusted.

drafts.title: The Art Deco cocktail cabinet
drafts.educational_claim: The 1920s–30s cocktail cabinet is a fitted machine for mixing at home — veneer, lacquer, chrome, glass, a drop or a slide — and it is a form, not a brand.

drafts.title: Repeal night and the new homework of mixing
drafts.educational_claim: Repeal on December 5, 1933, did not invent the home cocktail. It made the homework public, and furniture was allowed to be a mixing station instead of a hide.

drafts.title: The fitted cocktail machine of the 1930s
drafts.educational_claim: 1930s bar furniture is an interior architecture of small parts — racks, wells, leaves, lights — closer to a fitted kitchen than to a chest of drawers.

drafts.title: Wheels — the bar cart as hospitality
drafts.educational_claim: A bar cart is a cellarette that got taller and thinner. Mobility is the job. If it cannot roll and stop, it is a shelf with wheels for a photograph.

drafts.title: Credenzas that opened into a party
drafts.educational_claim: A mid-century credenza bar is a dry cabinet that kept parlor manners on the outside and a cocktail interior on the inside. The surprise is a door, not a trick latch.

drafts.title: The suburban wet bar and the rec room
drafts.educational_claim: The postwar rec-room wet bar is plumbing plus a counter in a room invented for informal company. It is a built-in habit, not a piece of parlor furniture.

drafts.title: Paneled dens, sunken floors, and the 1970s bar
drafts.educational_claim: 1970s den bars doubled down on room-as-tavern: dark paneling, mirrors, sunken floors. The furniture became interior architecture, and the architecture has a step you can miss in the dark.

drafts.title: Hotel brass leaking into the house
drafts.educational_claim: Brass footrails, speed rails, and back-bar mirrors are restaurant parts. A house can borrow them if it borrows the wipe-down. They are not required for a liquor cabinet.

drafts.title: Furniture against a built-in — the joint that decides
drafts.educational_claim: A piece of furniture is finished as an object and can leave on a truck. A built-in is scribed to the building. The joint, the back, and the calendar decide which one you asked for.

drafts.title: A wet bar is plumbing that hired a cabinetmaker
drafts.educational_claim: Wet means supply, waste, and a basin. The wood is a jacket around a licensed wet trade. Draw the drain before you draw the door.

drafts.title: The honest dry cabinet
drafts.educational_claim: A dry liquor cabinet is casegoods: no basin, no drain, a landing, a fitted interior. It is the object a furniture shop can put on a truck without hiring a plumber.

drafts.title: Butler's pantry revival versus the living-room bar
drafts.educational_claim: A modern "butler's pantry" is often a second kitchen or a display corridor. A living-room bar is hospitality in the sitting room. Putting both words on one wall usually ruins both jobs.

drafts.title: When the kitchen ate the dining room and kept the bottles
drafts.educational_claim: Open kitchens absorbed the dining-room performance. Bottles landed on islands and in appliance garages. That is convenient and hostile to furniture, labels, and heat.

drafts.title: Glass, stone, LED — the contemporary millwork bar
drafts.educational_claim: A contemporary millwork bar is a built-in of glass doors, stone, and light. The glow is easy. The heat, the reflections, and the stone edge are the job.

drafts.title: Bottle geometry — measure the object, then draw the box
drafts.educational_claim: A 750 ml bottle is roughly a foot tall and three inches across, until it is not. Cabinets fail when they are drawn from a mood board instead of the client's bottles.

drafts.title: Glassware, stems, and the rattle
drafts.educational_claim: Stemware is taller than memory and louder than a drawing. Hanging racks steal height. Thin cases rattle. Design the glass as a second collection, not as a decoration.

drafts.title: Seeing the bottles without cooking them
drafts.educational_claim: Interior light is heat and spectrum. LED is the current low-heat habit. A cabinet is not a display case at a fair. If you can cook a label, you designed a lamp, not a bar.

drafts.title: Hardware — locks, slides, and the ghost of 1925
drafts.educational_claim: Bar hardware is load-bearing: leaves, slides, hinges, locks. A trick latch is a costume. A slide that holds a pour is a tool.

drafts.title: Finish that has to live with alcohol and citrus
drafts.educational_claim: Bar tops and interiors are a hostile climate: ethanol, citric acid, water, ice. A jewelry finish is the wrong cousin. The film is a system, not a color.

drafts.title: Tops — wood, stone, and the wet line
drafts.educational_claim: The top is a working climate. Wood can work if the film is honest. Stone works if the stone matches the household. The wet line — sink, splash, seam — is where tops fail.

drafts.title: The cold machine you hide — and why it needs to breathe
drafts.educational_claim: Built-in refrigeration is usually front-venting and sized to a cutout on a sheet. Boxing a freestanding unit is how a cabinetmaker kills a compressor and then gets blamed.

drafts.title: A closed cabinet is a climate
drafts.educational_claim: A closed case has humidity, smell, heat, and mold opinions. Lids and doors are climate controls. A bar that cannot breathe or be wiped will become a cellar in the wrong sense.

drafts.title: Built-in versus a piece we can put on a truck
drafts.educational_claim: Company trucks are a design constraint. Split tops, finished backs, and racking loads are furniture. Scribes, site joints, and unfinished backs are built-ins. Do not make one drawing do both.

drafts.title: Codes, GFCI, and what this shop will not pretend to be
drafts.educational_claim: A furniture shop can wrap a wet bar. It cannot be the plumber, the electrician, or the code book. Local licenses beat a well-told cabinet story.

drafts.title: How to read a room before anyone draws a bar
drafts.educational_claim: Before a drawing, walk the room with bottles, water, and a path in mind. The history was a map of objects. The shop is a map of duties. The room decides which object is honest.
